threads_text: Google's own help page spells out the NotebookLM vs Gemini difference: Gemini Notebook answers only from your sources, the Gemini app can also pull in web search. Same notebooks, different rules. Which one would you trust with your notes?

site_article.answer_summary: Use Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM) when answers must come only from your files and you want Audio Overviews, flashcards or quizzes. Use the Gemini app when you want your notebook plus web search.

paragraphs.text: NotebookLM vs Gemini comes down to one choice: answers only from your own files, or answers that may also use the web. Google's help pages now call NotebookLM Gemini Notebook, an AI research assistant that answers from the sources you upload, with in-line citations. The Gemini app is the general assistant, and since this year it can open the same notebooks.

The short version: use Gemini Notebook when the answer must stay inside your documents and you want study tools like Audio Overviews, flashcards and quizzes. Use the Gemini app when you want to mix your notebook with web search and Gemini's other tools. The notebooks themselves are shared between the two apps, so you do not have to pick only one.
NotebookLM vs Gemini: the one difference that matters

Google's own help page states it plainly. In Gemini Notebook, answers are grounded only in your notebook sources. In the Gemini app, answers are grounded in your notebook sources but may also include web search and other tools. Gemini Notebook is designed to answer from the information in what you uploaded, and every answer carries citations you can click back to the source.

Chalkbox, a study site that tested both, sums it up the same way: the notebook answers only from your sources, the app answers from everything. It also adds a fair warning: grounding cuts down on made up facts, but the model can still misread a document. Check the citation before you quote anything.

That makes the choice easy in practice. Writing about assigned readings, a contract, or meeting notes where a made up fact would hurt you: Gemini Notebook. Explaining a concept your files do not cover, or checking something against the current web: the Gemini app.
How notebooks work across both apps

Notebooks you create in Gemini Notebook now show up automatically in the Gemini app's navigation, and you can view, edit and chat with them from either side. Renaming a notebook, adding sources, or changing its custom instructions syncs between the two apps. If a change does not show up, Google suggests refreshing. Both apps share one set of custom instructions per notebook.

There are a few catches. Shared notebooks made in Gemini Notebook, even ones you own, do not appear in the Gemini app. A notebook that contains Gemini chats is private and cannot be shared. Play Books ebooks can only be added as sources in Gemini Notebook. In the European Economic Area you have to connect Gemini Notebook to Gemini by hand; in most other regions it connects automatically.
What only Gemini Notebook can do

The Studio panel is the big reason to open Gemini Notebook itself. Google lists Notes, Audio Overviews, Video Overviews, Mind Maps, Reports (FAQ, study guide or briefing document, with Export to Docs), Data Tables (Export to Sheets), Flashcards, Quizzes, Slide Decks and Infographics. The Gemini app cannot generate these Studio items: Google says they are only available in Gemini Notebook.

Audio Overviews turn your sources into a discussion between AI hosts. You can pick Deep Dive (the default), The Brief (one speaker, under two minutes), The Critique or The Debate, choose the length, and add a prompt about what to focus on. In English you can also use Interactive mode and join the conversation to ask questions. It works in more than 80 languages.

Flashcards and Quizzes turn your sources into study aids. You can set the difficulty to easy, medium or hard, choose fewer, standard or more cards, and add a prompt. Flashcards have Got it! and Missed it! buttons, so you can review only the cards you missed, and you can download the deck as a CSV file.
What the Gemini app adds

In the Gemini app, a notebook chat can use web searches and any Gemini tool, and Gemini remembers the context of your sources and instructions. You can ask Gemini in plain words to create, edit or delete notebooks, add or remove sources, or list your notebooks. Sources can be files from your device (PDFs, documents, spreadsheets, images, audio and text files), Google Drive files, websites and copied text. Google says you can add up to 600 sources, depending on your Google AI plan.

The Gemini app also has study notebooks on the web at gemini.google.com, with diagnostic quizzes, personalized lessons and progress tracking. They need Gemini Apps Activity (History) turned on and are not yet in the mobile app.
How to start a notebook in each app

paragraphs.title: 1. Gemini Notebook: create the notebook
paragraphs.text: Open Gemini Notebook and select Create new notebook. In the pop up, select Upload a source. You can add PDFs, websites, YouTube videos, audio files, Google Docs or Google Slides. Add more later with the + Add button.

paragraphs.title: 2. Gemini Notebook: open Studio
paragraphs.text: Once your sources are in, use the Chat panel for questions and the Studio panel on the side for Audio Overviews, Mind Maps, Reports, Flashcards or Quizzes. A few starter items are made automatically when you first add sources, and Google says those do not count toward your limits.

paragraphs.title: 3. Gemini app: make a notebook
paragraphs.text: On gemini.google.com or in the Gemini mobile app, tap Menu at the top left, then New notebook under Notebooks. Give it a name, type a prompt and tap Add sources.

paragraphs.title: 4. Gemini app: talk to an existing notebook
paragraphs.text: Type @Gemini Notebook in a prompt to connect the app the first time, then ask about any notebook by name. To file a normal Gemini chat into a notebook, open More, then Add to notebook. This needs Keep Activity turned on.

paragraphs.title: Prompt 1: Check a claim against your files only (Gemini Notebook)
paragraphs.text: Using only my sources, list every place that mentions [topic]. For each one, quote the key sentence and say which source it is from. If my sources do not cover it, say so instead of guessing.

paragraphs.title: Prompt 2: Mix your notes with the web (Gemini app)
paragraphs.text: Read my notebook [notebook name]. Summarize what my notes say about [topic], then search the web for anything newer and tell me clearly which points come from my notes and which come from the web.
Limits and plans

Gemini Notebook's limits are compute based, so they depend on how complex your prompt is, which features you use and how long the chat gets. Your quota refreshes every 5 hours until you hit a weekly limit. Without a plan you get standard limits. Google AI Plus doubles them, AI Pro gives four times the standard limit, and AI Ultra gives 5 or 20 times the AI Pro limit, depending on the subscription. You can check your usage under Settings, then Usage.

Gemini Notebook is available in the browser to users above the age of consent in their country, in a long list of countries that includes the US, the UK, Canada, Australia and India. Most work and school Google accounts have access if their admin turns it on. Google says files and chats in Gemini Notebook are not used to train its foundation models unless you send feedback.

Deleting is not the same everywhere. Google's pages say deleting a notebook removes its sources, so download anything you want to keep, such as flashcards as CSV or reports exported to Docs, before you delete.

Our take: for most people the answer to NotebookLM vs Gemini is both. Build the notebook in Gemini Notebook, where the Studio tools live and the answers stay inside your files. Open the same notebook in the Gemini app when you need the web or Gemini's other tools on top. The only real mistake is asking the Gemini app something that must come only from your documents and trusting the answer without checking where it came from.
